MEDI2200 · Week 4 · Meiosis — Dr Lucinda McRobb

Meiosis — halving the genome, then reshuffling it

Last week's mitosis copied the genome exactly. Meiosis does the opposite: it halves the chromosome number to make gametes, and along the way deliberately mixes the genome so no two offspring are alike. This guide follows the module from why meiosis exists to the errors (non-disjunction) that cause aneuploidy — using its own figures.

Covers 3 learning objectives Figures 7 plates from your module Recall 5 section checklists

§0Purpose · LO1

Why meiosis

To make haploid gametes — and to mix the genome doing it.

Sexual reproduction fuses two cells into one. If those cells carried the full diploid (2n) genome, the chromosome number would double every generation. Meiosis solves this: it divides germ cells (in the ovaries and testes) into haploid (n) gametes, so that fertilisation restores the diploid number — and it uses the opportunity to reshuffle the genome. Plate 0.1 is the whole cycle.

Label Key — the diploid ↔ haploid cycle
Diploid germ cell (2n)
The starting cell in the ovary/testis — full chromosome set.
Meiosis / gametogenesis
Spermatogenesis (sperm) or oogenesis (ova) — halves the genome to n.
Haploid gametes (n)
The specialised reproductive cells: sperm or ovum.
Fertilisation (2n)
Fusion of egg + sperm restores the diploid number — and combines two genomes (genetic variation).
Reasoning · halving is the whole point

Fertilisation is addition, so meiosis has to be subtraction. Two haploid gametes (n + n) make one diploid zygote (2n); if gametes stayed diploid, every generation would carry twice the chromosomes of the last. That single constraint — keep the species' chromosome number constant across generations — is why a reductional division exists at all, and why it's confined to germ cells (somatic cells never need to halve).

Memory hook · the ploidy cycle

Meiosis halves (2n → n), fertilisation doubles back (n + n → 2n). Gametes are the only human cells that are haploid.

R Recall checklist — why meiosis
  • Purpose — make haploid gametes so fertilisation restores 2n (and mix the genome).
  • Where — germ cells (ovaries, testes); gametogenesis = spermatogenesis / oogenesis.
  • Fertilisation — n gamete + n gamete → 2n zygote.
§1Comparison · LO1

Meiosis vs mitosis

Same start (one replication) — opposite ends (identical vs varied).

Both divisions begin the same way — a single round of DNA replication — but then diverge completely. Mitosis divides once for two identical diploid daughters; meiosis divides twice for up to four varied haploid cells.

Mitosis vs meiosis
MitosisMeiosis
DNA replicationsOne (S phase)One (S phase)
DivisionsOneTwo (meiosis I & II)
Daughter cells2, diploid (2n)4, haploid (n)
GeneticsIdentical (conserved)Varied (reshuffled)
Homologues pair?NoYes (in prophase I)
WhereSomatic cellsGerm cells
Reasoning · one replication, two divisions = halving

The arithmetic is the key. A cell replicates its DNA once (going from 2n to 2n with doubled chromatids), then divides twice without replicating again. Two divisions on one replication necessarily quarters the DNA content and halves the chromosome number — that's how meiosis reaches haploid. Mitosis, with one division on one replication, simply returns to the diploid start.

Memory hook · tell them apart

Mitosis = identical (one division, 2 diploid). Meiosis = exchange/variation (two divisions, 4 haploid). Homologues pairing = you're in meiosis.

R Recall checklist — meiosis vs mitosis
  • Both — one DNA replication first.
  • Mitosis — 1 division → 2 identical diploid cells (somatic).
  • Meiosis — 2 divisions → 4 varied haploid cells (germ); homologues pair.
§2Stages · LO1

The stages of meiosis I & II

Two divisions: first separate the pairs, then split the copies.

After one replication in interphase (each chromosome now two sister chromatids), meiosis runs two divisions. Plate 2.1 gives the big picture: meiosis I separates the homologous chromosomes, and meiosis II separates the sister chromatids.

Label Key — two rounds, two separations
Start
A diploid cell whose replicated chromosomes each hold two sister chromatids.
Meiosis I — homologues separate
The homologous pair splits → two haploid cells, but each chromosome is still two chromatids (reductional).
Meiosis II — sister chromatids separate
Like mitosis, the sisters split → four haploid cells with single, unreplicated chromosomes.

Plate 2.2 walks through both divisions phase by phase — PMAT I then PMAT II. The critical difference from mitosis is anaphase I: the homologues are pulled apart while the sister chromatids stay together.

Label Key — the two rounds
PMAT I
Prophase I → Metaphase I → Anaphase I → Telophase I: the homologous pairs (23) align and then separate.
PMAT II
Prophase II → Metaphase II → Anaphase II → Telophase II: the sister chromatids align and separate (just like mitosis).
Result
Four haploid cells from one starting cell.
Reasoning · why two different divisions

Halving needs a step mitosis doesn't have: pulling apart the homologues, not the sister chromatids. So meiosis I is the novel, reductional division (homologues separate → haploid), and meiosis II is essentially a mitosis of those haploid cells (sisters separate). Get one thing right and the rest follows: anaphase I = homologues apart; anaphase II = sisters apart.

Memory hook · I vs II

Meiosis I = separate the pairs (homologues) — the "reduction." Meiosis II = separate the chromatids — a "mitosis" of haploid cells. "Pairs first, copies second."

R Recall checklist — the stages
  • One replication (interphase) → two divisions, no replication between.
  • Meiosis I (PMAT I) — homologues pair & separate → haploid cells, still 2 chromatids each (reductional).
  • Meiosis II (PMAT II) — sister chromatids separate → 4 haploid cells, single chromosomes.
  • Anaphase I = homologues apart; anaphase II = sisters apart.
§3Genetic variation · LO2

Three sources of genetic variation

Cross over, then assort at random — twice.

Meiosis doesn't just halve — it reshuffles. It builds genetic variation three separate ways: crossing over in prophase I, and independent assortment in metaphase I and again in metaphase II. Plate 3.1 shows the first two on the phases of meiosis I.

Label Key — variation being built
Prophase I — crossing over
Homologous chromosomes pair and exchange fragments — recombining maternal and paternal alleles.
Metaphase I — alignment
The homologue pairs line up at the metaphase plate (their orientation is random — source 2).
Anaphase I
Homologues separate; sister chromatids stay together.
Telophase I
Haploid cells whose chromosomes are now non-identical sister chromatids (because of crossing over).

Source 1 — crossing over (prophase I)

Prophase I is long and has five substages (Plate 3.2). Homologues pair up (synapsis, forming a bivalent/tetrad), a synaptonemal complex forms, and non-sister chromatids exchange DNA. The crossover points, visible once the complex dissolves, are chiasmata (singular chiasma) — and without chiasmata, chromosome segregation can go wrong (§4).

Label Key — prophase I substages
Leptotene → Zygotene
Chromosomes condense; homologues pair (synapsis) via the synaptonemal complex.
Pachytene
Crossing over — non-sister chromatids exchange DNA.
Diplotene
The complex dissolves but the crossovers remain visible as chiasmata.
Diakinesis
Full condensation; the nuclear membrane disintegrates, ready for metaphase.

Sources 2 & 3 — independent assortment (metaphase I & II)

Source 2 — metaphase I: each homologous pair orients on the metaphase plate independently and at random, so every gamete inherits a random mix of maternal and paternal homologues. Source 3 — metaphase II (Plate 3.3): because crossing over made the sister chromatids non-identical, their random orientation in the second division adds a third layer of variation.

Label Key — the third source
Line up at the metaphase plate
The (now non-identical) chromatids orient randomly in meiosis II.
Sister chromatids separate
They are pulled to opposite ends — but because they differ (crossing over), the daughters differ too.
Reasoning · why these give astronomical variety

Each mechanism multiplies the last. Independent assortment alone gives 2²³ (≈8 million) possible homologue combinations per gamete — and that's before crossing over, which makes each chromosome a unique maternal/paternal mosaic, and before the metaphase-II shuffle of those now-unique chromatids. Multiply the three and essentially no two gametes (and no two siblings) are ever genetically identical — the biological engine of diversity.

Memory hook · the three sources

Cross over (prophase I) · Assort homologues (metaphase I) · Assort non-identical chromatids (metaphase II). "One crossover, two random line-ups."

R Recall checklist — genetic variation
  • 1. Crossing over (prophase I) — synapsis → chiasmata; non-sister chromatids exchange DNA.
  • Prophase I substages — leptotene, zygotene, pachytene, diplotene, diakinesis.
  • 2. Independent assortment (metaphase I) — random orientation of homologue pairs.
  • 3. Random assortment (metaphase II) — of the now non-identical sister chromatids.
§4Non-disjunction · LO3

Non-disjunction & aneuploidy

When separation fails, a gamete ends up with one too many — or too few.

Non-disjunction is the failure of chromosomes to separate properly — homologues failing to separate in meiosis I, or sister chromatids failing in meiosis II. Either way, a gamete ends up with an extra or a missing chromosome, so after fertilisation the individual is aneuploid (a wrong chromosome number). Chiasmata are needed for correct segregation, so failure to form them is one cause.

Where non-disjunction happens
Failure in…What doesn't separateResult
Meiosis IHomologous chromosomesGametes with an extra / missing chromosome
Meiosis IISister chromatidsGametes with an extra / missing chromosome

Plate 4.1 shows the clinical consequences on a karyotype — an extra autosome, or an abnormal sex-chromosome count.

Label Key — two aneuploidies
Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome)
Three copies of autosome 21 — increased gene dosage with developmental consequences.
Monosomy X (Turner, 45,X)
A single X chromosome — 45 chromosomes instead of 46, with developmental and reproductive effects.
(Also 47,XXY)
Klinefelter syndrome — an extra X in a male.
Reasoning · why chiasmata prevent errors

Chiasmata aren't only for variation — they're the physical tether that keeps homologous pairs joined and correctly oriented until anaphase I. A pair with no chiasma can drift and be pulled to the same pole, i.e. non-disjunction. So the very event that creates diversity (crossing over) also safeguards accurate segregation — which is why failed crossing over is one route to aneuploidy.

Clinical / real-world · aneuploidy in medicine

Non-disjunction is the commonest source of clinically important chromosome disorders. Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) is the most frequent autosomal aneuploidy; its risk rises with maternal age, reflecting errors in the long-arrested oocyte's meiosis I. Sex-chromosome aneuploidies — Turner (45,X) and Klinefelter (47,XXY) — are generally milder because of X-inactivation (dosage compensation, §W3). This is exactly what prenatal karyotyping and non-invasive prenatal testing screen for.

Memory hook · non-disjunction

Non-disjunction = "didn't split." M-I fails → whole homologues misdivide; M-II fails → sister chromatids misdivide. Extra chromosome = trisomy (21 = Down); missing = monosomy (X = Turner).

R Recall checklist — non-disjunction
  • Non-disjunction — failure to separate: homologues (meiosis I) or sister chromatids (meiosis II).
  • Result — gametes with extra/missing chromosomes → aneuploid offspring.
  • Trisomy 21 = Down (47,+21); monosomy X = Turner (45,X); 47,XXY = Klinefelter.
  • Chiasmata tether homologues for correct segregation — failed crossover is one cause.
